source.title: JBShield: Defending Large Language Models from Jailbreak Attacks through Activated Concept Analysis and Manipulation
source.authors: Shenyi Zhang; Yu-Chen Zhai; Keyan Guo; Hong-Xin Hu; Sheng-Nan Guo; Zheng Fang; Ling-Chen Zhao; Chao Shen; Cong Wang; Qian Wang

record.tranche_reason: Evaluates whether jailbreak prompts make safety-aligned chat models comply, including suffix-based attacks, but does not test fine-tuning or response-position KL.
record.gate_note: Table 7 reports attack success rates without defense for each model and attack; these directly bear on whether jailbreak attacks bypass refusal. Results for JBShield-M and other new defenses are not cataloged as claim results. The concept-extraction discussion is recorded separately as a finding outside the listed versions.
record.test_reason: A jailbreak-defense paper. As its no-defense baseline, it reports attack success rates (Table 7) of the suffix attacks GCG and SAA on five aligned chat models, judged by SORRY-Bench. These bear on V4's suffix clause in a new setting. The other seven attacks (IJP, AutoDAN, PAIR, DrAttack, Puzzler, Zulu, Base64) are template, rewrite or encoding jailbreaks, not opening, suffix or decoding manipulations, so they do not measure what V4 names. No fine-tuning, per-token KL, parameter localization or deepening is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that aligned LLMs still recognize toxic concepts inside jailbreak prompts, and that jailbreaks work by activating a separate jailbreak concept that shifts output toward compliance. They report that JBShield detects jailbreaks with 0.95 average accuracy and cuts average ASR from 61% to 2%.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes jailbreak prompt representations and manipulates hidden activations as a defense; it does not fine-tune on harmful or benign examples or measure per-token KL.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack type and target model change the no-defense attack success rate.

fits_no_version.finding: Concept extraction finds that jailbreak prompts still activate toxic-concept directions but add a 'jailbreak concept' whose top tokens are compliance words such as 'sure' and 'yes'.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Jailbreaks leave harm recognition intact and add a separate compliance direction in the representation space.

record.problems: The paper reports no uncertainty intervals for the ASRs. It uses SORRY-Bench for most attack evaluations and manual evaluation for Zulu and Base64; its appendix notes that SORRY-Bench performs poorly on encoding-based attacks. Some attack/model conditions have low or zero ASR, and the authors note dependence on model internals and calibration-data quality.
record.rows_left_out: No Table 7 no-defense ASR results were omitted. JBShield-M and baseline defense comparisons, Table 8 ablations, Table 9 adaptive attacks under the defense, and detection accuracy results were left out because they measure the study's defense or detection method rather than the claim's bypass behaviour.

untested.parts: Prefilling a compliant start and decoding changes; only GCG and SAA suffix attacks are tested.
Parameter or rank localization. The study edits activations at a single layer, not weights.
Causes of shallowness in data or objective.

missing.what: No-defense unsafe-response rates on plain harmful prompts. These are the no-attack baseline for the Table 7 rows: Mistral 0.30/0.10, Vicuna-7B 0.07/0.00, Vicuna-13B 0.00/0.00, Llama2 0.00/0.00, Llama3 0.03/0.00 (AdvBench/HEx-PHI).

record.verdict_notes: Defense paper; the claim-relevant results are only its no-defense baselines. Table 7 ASRs are on 50 prompts per cell, with no uncertainty reported. SORRY-Bench was the judge, except manual judging for Zulu and Base64. GCG and SAA prompts were regenerated per target model with default settings, so SAA's lower Llama ASR may reflect setup rather than the original attack's strength. No prefilling experiments.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful fine-tuning and its effects on refusal.
Benign fine-tuning and its effects on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models across response positions.
Prefilled compliant openings and decoding changes. Tests suffix-based GCG and SAA, as well as other jailbreak prompt attacks.
Whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
Whether safety-training data or objectives produce first-token shallowness.
Training safety beyond the first tokens and whether it remains robust.

rows.subject: Mistral-7B
rows.operation_detail: Extract and interpret toxic and jailbreak concepts from prompt representations.
rows.measure: Interpretable concept tokens and stated concept interpretation
rows.value: Authors report similar toxic-concept tokens for harmful and jailbreak prompts, and compliance-related tokens for jailbreak concepts; they interpret the latter as shifting outputs toward compliance.
rows.note: This is the authors' proposed mechanism for jailbreak effects, not a test of first-token concentration or training-induced shallowness.
